questions.q: A student writes: "I am a bad friend because I forgot my best friend's birthday." Identify which part of this statement reflects self-concept and which reflects self-esteem, and explain the difference in one sentence each.
questions.a: Self-concept: "I forgot my best friend's birthday" (descriptive, factual claim about behaviour). Self-esteem: "I am a bad friend" (evaluative judgment of worth based on that behaviour). A wrong answer that labels both as self-concept reveals the student cannot separate factual self-descriptions from value-laden self-evaluations — a critical error because board questions ask to "distinguish with examples."

questions.q: "Self-esteem is simply the sum of all positive self-concept statements." Critique this statement using the NCERT definition of self-esteem as "judgment according to standards we have set for ourselves which are largely influenced by society."
questions.a: The statement is incorrect because self-esteem is not a mathematical sum of positive traits; it is a *subjective evaluation* against *internalised standards* (which may be unrealistic). A student with many positive self-concept traits ("I am smart, kind, talented") can have low self-esteem if their ideal self demands perfection. A wrong answer that agrees reveals the misconception that self-esteem = positive self-concept, ignoring the role of standards and the real-ideal discrepancy central to NCERT.

questions.q: Priya (16) describes herself as "average in studies, good at painting, short-tempered." She feels "okay" about herself. Rahul (16) describes himself identically but feels "like a failure." Using the self-concept/self-esteem relationship, explain why their self-esteem differs despite identical self-concepts.
questions.a: Priya's ideal-self standards are likely aligned with her real self (she accepts "average" as sufficient), so the real-ideal discrepancy is small → positive self-esteem. Rahul's ideal self likely demands "top grades, calm temperament," creating a large real-ideal discrepancy → negative self-esteem. A wrong answer attributing the difference solely to the self-concept content shows failure to grasp that self-esteem depends on the *evaluation against standards*, not the content alone.

questions.q: Analyse how the developmental shift from middle childhood (concrete, comparative self-descriptions) to adolescence (abstract, contradictory self-descriptions) complicates the self-concept → self-esteem relationship. Give one concrete example.
questions.a: In middle childhood, self-concept is concrete ("I run faster than Kiran") allowing clear, stable self-evaluation. In adolescence, abstract and contradictory self-concepts ("I am shy but also want to lead") create *ambiguous standards* for evaluation — the adolescent cannot easily judge if they meet "being a leader" when they also see themselves as "shy." This ambiguity causes fluctuating self-esteem. A wrong answer focusing only on "abstract thinking" without linking to *evaluative instability* misses the core mechanism.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "Improving self-esteem requires only changing negative self-concept statements to positive ones (e.g., 'I am stupid' → 'I am smart')." Consider the role of internalised societal standards and the real-ideal gap.
questions.a: The claim is flawed because (1) positive affirmations that contradict lived experience ("I am smart" when failing exams) increase cognitive dissonance, lowering self-esteem further; (2) self-esteem depends on *perceived congruence* between real self and *internalised standards*, not mere positivity. If societal standards equate worth with academic marks, changing self-talk without addressing the standard or the performance gap fails. A wrong answer endorsing affirmations ignores the NCERT emphasis on "standards largely influenced by society" and the real-ideal discrepancy mechanism.

questions.q: Create a 3-statement "I am..." profile for an adolescent that would *maximise* the risk of low self-esteem according to the self-concept/self-esteem discrepancy model. Justify each statement's contribution.
questions.a: Example: (1) "I am invisible in class" (global negative self-concept), (2) "I must be popular to be worthy" (unrealistic, externally dependent ideal-self standard), (3) "I never get anything right" (distorted self-concept ignoring competencies). Justification: Statement 1 creates a negative real self; Statement 2 sets an unattainable ideal self dependent on others; Statement 3 prevents recognition of evidence that could narrow the gap. A poor answer lists negative traits without linking to *standards* or *discrepancy*, showing rote memorisation of "negative = bad" without mechanistic understanding.
